slides.title: An allocator promises valid regions, not just a free-byte total
keyPoints: Live payloads must not overlap
Size and alignment must both fit
Release must refer to a valid allocation identity
slides.narration: A caller asking for twelve bytes needs one usable region satisfying the allocator's alignment and lifetime contract. Twelve free bytes scattered in unrelated gaps may not be enough. The allocator also stores metadata, and the complete managed block can be larger than the requested payload. Before studying selection algorithms, state the core promises: live payloads do not overlap, returned storage meets the declared size and alignment, and valid release returns a block to the allocator exactly once. A teaching allocator can have a narrow single-threaded contract. Calling it an allocator does not automatically make it a replacement for every guarantee supplied by a production memory system.
actions: State the non-overlap invariant before discussing any search policy.

question.prompt: Why can total free bytes exceed a request while allocation still fails?
question.answer: The free bytes may be split into regions too small to satisfy one contiguous, suitably aligned request.

slides.title: Best fit describes one local choice
keyPoints: First fit depends on list order
Best fit minimizes the immediate chosen remainder
Future requests and search costs still matter
slides.narration: Suppose the candidate free block sizes are thirty, eighteen, and twenty-four, and the request is sixteen. First fit chooses thirty if that is the list order, while best fit chooses eighteen. Best fit leaves a smaller immediate remainder, but its name does not prove that the future workload will use memory better. A two-byte fragment may be less useful than a larger one, and finding the smallest candidate may require more search or a more complex index. Compare policies with complete request-and-release traces and clear metrics. A single attractive allocation is not enough evidence for a global performance or fragmentation claim.
actions: Predict the chosen sizes for request 16 before showing the program.

question.prompt: What does best fit optimize in the immediate selection step?
question.answer: It chooses the smallest available candidate large enough for the request, not a guaranteed best future allocation history.

slides.title: Compare selection policies with a transparent model
keyPoints: The array contains candidate sizes, not managed memory
First eligible candidate is 30
Smallest eligible candidate is 18
slides.narration: This program models only block selection. It does not hand out actual payload pointers or measure allocator speed. The loop records the first candidate that fits and separately tracks the smallest fitting candidate. For a request of sixteen, it prints first fit=30 with remainder=14, then best fit=18 with remainder=2. The sentinel index equals the array size until a candidate exists, and the program checks that state before indexing the results. A production allocator must do more: account for metadata and alignment, decide whether a remainder can become a valid free block, and update ownership records. Isolating selection helps us see what each policy really promises.
actions: Run after predicting both selected sizes, then list the omitted allocator obligations.

slides.title: A live block separates free capacity into unusable pieces
keyPoints: The model has three consecutive eight-byte regions
Two free ends total 16 but the largest run is 8
Releasing the middle permits a 24-byte run
slides.narration: The region records explicitly model physical order in one managed area; they are not an arbitrary free-list order. Initially, the middle eight bytes are live. The two free ends total sixteen bytes, but the largest contiguous free run is only eight, so a twelve-byte request prints false. After the middle region is marked free, the adjacent free run is twenty-four and the same fit test prints true. This is a model of external fragmentation and the opportunity for coalescing. No live object is moved, and no actual allocation takes place. The key condition is physical adjacency with no live region between the free pieces.
actions: Trace the running total resetting at the live middle region before Run.

question.prompt: Why could the two free end regions not be merged before the middle release?
question.answer: A live region separates them. Merging across it would overlap or destroy an existing allocation’s payload.

slides.title: Where the simple approach fails
keyPoints: Advancing by the requested byte count alone can violate alignment. The rounding formula also needs overflow checks for unbounded inputs.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Update used before checking the request. A rejected allocation then consumes or corrupts the remaining arena state.

The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Compute candidate offsets in local values and commit used only after the last bound check. Test failure after one successful allocation.

slides.title: Mechanism, guarantees, and limits
keyPoints: Padding is computed separately and checked against remaining space before addition. The state changes only after every bound passes, which makes failure leave the arena usable. Returning an optional offset distinguishes rejection from a valid start at zero. This bump model has no individual free operation and does not create C++ objects in raw storage.
A plausible alternative: Use normal containers or a standard allocator unless measured allocation costs or a shared lifetime justify a custom arena.

slides.title: Blocks
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A block is a unit of storage managed by the allocator.
It may contain a header, a payload returned to the caller, and padding.
The caller’s requested size and the allocator’s actual block size can differ.
A 13-byte request might occupy a larger block because of alignment or size classes.
slides.narration: A block is a unit of storage managed by the allocator. It may contain a header, a payload returned to the caller, and padding. The caller’s requested size and the allocator’s actual block size can differ. A 13-byte request might occupy a larger block because of alignment or size classes. The fundamental invariant is that live allocation payloads do not overlap and remain valid until release. A custom allocator should state its supported alignments, maximum request size, zero-size policy, and threading model. Without those declarations, callers cannot know whether a returned address is appropriate for their object.

slides.title: Metadata
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Metadata records information such as block size, allocation state, neighboring blocks, or free-list links.
It can be stored next to the payload or in separate tables.
Adjacent metadata is convenient but can be corrupted by an out-of-bounds write from the payload.
Never treat allocator metadata as trustworthy after detecting memory corruption.
slides.narration: Metadata records information such as block size, allocation state, neighboring blocks, or free-list links. It can be stored next to the payload or in separate tables. Adjacent metadata is convenient but can be corrupted by an out-of-bounds write from the payload. Never treat allocator metadata as trustworthy after detecting memory corruption. Continuing to allocate and free through damaged state can amplify the failure. A teaching allocator can use assertions and validation scans; a production allocator also needs careful hardening, concurrency control, and recovery policy. Implementing an allocator is not just writing a fast search loop.

Headers and alignment padding may be reported separately or included; consistency matters.

Compaction could move live objects, but ordinary raw pointers make transparent movement difficult.

slides.title: A bounded bump arena
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: The requirement is to allocate aligned byte regions from a fixed 128-byte arena and reject requests that do not fit.

slides.narration: The requirement is to allocate aligned byte regions from a fixed 128-byte arena and reject requests that do not fit. Individual release is intentionally unsupported. The arena provides storage only; the example does not construct nontrivial objects inside it. Companion listing: ch10/arena.cpp The first request consumes three bytes. On the stated alignment model, the next eight-byte-aligned start is offset 8, so five padding bytes are skipped and the second payload occupies offsets 8 through 15. The cursor becomes 16. The 200-byte request cannot fit and leaves the cursor unchanged. The abstraction has deliberately narrow semantics. Returned regions remain valid only until reset or destruction, and the arena is not thread-safe. A complete object allocator would add construction, destruction, and stronger alignment policy. Keeping the storage-only contract explicit makes this example useful without presenting it as a drop-in replacement for the standard allocator.

slides.title: A free list is a representation of allocator state
keyPoints: Free blocks appear once
Live blocks must not remain eligible
Metadata updates must preserve consistency
slides.narration: An explicit free list helps the allocator find reusable regions without scanning every live block. Its usefulness depends on its bookkeeping being true. A block appearing twice can be handed out twice. A live block accidentally left on the list can overlap a new allocation. Links stored in a free payload are metadata, not bytes the old caller may continue modifying after release. In a teaching implementation, a validation scan can check uniqueness, region bounds, non-overlap, and agreement between physical blocks and free-list entries. A concurrent implementation adds synchronization obligations to those same invariants. Fast lookup is not valuable if the structure describing available storage is wrong.
actions: Ask learners to connect each bookkeeping rule to a possible overlapping allocation.

question.prompt: What concrete failure can follow from one block appearing twice in a free list?
question.answer: The allocator can select the same storage for two live requests, violating the non-overlap invariant.

slides.title: Split only when the remainder is a valid block
keyPoints: Account for the entire allocated block
Check the minimum reusable remainder
Update physical neighbors and free-list entries together
slides.narration: Consider a sixty-four-byte free block under a policy requiring every remaining free block to occupy at least thirty-two bytes. If the accounted allocated block needs thirty-two, splitting leaves another valid thirty-two-byte block. If it needs forty-eight, the remaining sixteen is too small under this policy, so giving the whole block to the request may be correct. That extra reserved space is internal waste rather than a separately reusable region. Real accounting must include headers and alignment, not only the caller's payload bytes. The split also changes neighbor boundaries and list membership. Trace all those updates before publishing the new allocator state to a caller.
actions: Compare the 32-byte and 48-byte accounted requests under the same minimum-remainder rule.

question.prompt: Why might a larger free block be allocated whole instead of split?
question.answer: The remainder may be too small to hold a valid reusable block with required metadata, alignment, and minimum payload.

slides.title: Align the payload and count the gap before it
keyPoints: The header’s alignment alone is insufficient
Padding consumes capacity
Reject before updating the used cursor
slides.narration: An arena cursor at offset seventeen under an eight-byte alignment needs seven bytes of padding before the next payload can begin at twenty-four. In a thirty-two-byte region, only eight payload bytes then remain. A request for nine must fail even though fifteen bytes were unused before alignment. Check the gap and payload against remaining capacity before changing the cursor. A header placed before the payload can introduce another offset that must be included. std::align can help locate an aligned subregion within supplied storage, but it neither obtains more storage nor constructs a C++ object. The caller and allocator must agree on both the alignment contract and the object-lifetime work.
actions: Compute padding, start, and remaining payload separately before deciding success.

question.prompt: At used=17 and capacity=32 with alignment 8, why does a nine-byte request fail?
question.answer: Seven bytes are needed to reach offset 24, leaving only eight bytes for payload. The pre-alignment free count alone is misleading.

slides.title: An arena trades individual release for a shared lifetime
keyPoints: A cursor can serve many small requests
Reset invalidates all backed objects and views
Nontrivial objects may still require destruction
slides.narration: An arena can make allocation simple by advancing a cursor through one region and resetting the whole region when a request or document is finished. That works well when the allocated objects share a lifetime. It is a poor match for independent long-lived objects that expect individual reclamation. Resetting the cursor does not preserve old borrowed views, and nontrivial C++ objects may require their destructors before their storage is reused. Returning an aligned offset is only a storage reservation model, not complete object construction. Keep the arena's lifetime boundary visible in the surrounding API so callers cannot accidentally retain a pointer into a later request's reused memory.
actions: Choose a parsed request as a good shared-lifetime case and contrast an independently retained object.

question.prompt: Why can an arena reset be unsafe even when no operating-system memory is freed?
question.answer: It ends the supported use of the old arena-backed objects and views and permits storage reuse; physical retention does not preserve their contract.

slides.title: Validate allocator structure after every mutation in teaching tests
keyPoints: Managed regions remain in bounds and non-overlapping
Each live allocation has one release identity
Rejected operations leave metadata consistent
slides.narration: A custom allocator needs tests of its internal structure, not just successful pointer returns. After each split, release, and merge, verify that blocks remain within the managed region, cover the intended accounted space, and do not overlap. Check that free-list membership matches block state and that coalescing removes old entries before inserting a combined region once. A rejected allocation should leave the previous metadata unchanged under the chosen contract. Test neighboring frees in different orders because adjacency bugs can hide in one convenient sequence. slides.narration: An allocator policy should be evaluated against the workload it will serve. Request sizes, release order, concurrency, and shared lifetimes affect search cost and fragmentation. Internal fragmentation counts unused space within allocated blocks under a stated accounting rule. External fragmentation concerns separated free regions that cannot satisfy a larger contiguous request. Headers and alignment may be counted separately, but the report must be consistent. Our models explain individual mechanisms; they do not measure production speed. Before replacing a standard allocator, identify the unmet requirement, define a narrow correct contract, and collect evidence that the new design improves the intended metric without breaking ownership or alignment guarantees.
